items.title: I can define wellbeing and distinguish it from mental wellbeing
items.what: Wellbeing is a state in which an individual is mentally, physically, and socially healthy and secure. Mental wellbeing is more specific and refers to an individual's psychological state, including their ability to think, process information, and regulate emotions.
items.why: Distinguishing between general wellbeing and mental wellbeing allows for precise discussion of psychological health, which is required for exam responses and clinical reasoning.
items.example: A person recovering from a broken leg may have low physical wellbeing but still demonstrate high mental wellbeing by maintaining a positive outlook, staying socially connected, and managing daily tasks effectively.

subtopic.name: What is Mental Wellbeing
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces the concept of mental wellbeing as a psychological state involving the ability to think, process information, and regulate emotions. It establishes that wellbeing is multifaceted and can be considered from several perspectives.
subtopic.why: Without a clear definition of mental wellbeing, it is impossible to measure, track, or support it. Understanding what wellbeing means provides the foundation for everything else in this topic.

items.title: I can identify the three main ways of considering mental wellbeing
items.what: Mental wellbeing can be considered through three lenses: levels of functioning, resilience, and social and emotional wellbeing. These are not separate conditions but interconnected aspects of the same overall state.
items.why: The VCE study design requires students to apply all three frameworks to scenarios. Recognising that they are interrelated, not independent, is essential for extended response questions.
items.example: In a VCAA exam scenario, a student who is unable to get out of bed (low functioning), avoids friends after a breakup (low social wellbeing), and feels overwhelmed by minor setbacks (low resilience) can be analysed using all three frameworks simultaneously.

subtopic.why: Without a clear definition of mental wellbeing, it is impossible to measure, track, or support it. Understanding what wellbeing means provides the foundation for everything else in this topic.

items.title: I can explain how mental wellbeing differs from the absence of mental illness
items.what: Mental wellbeing is not simply the absence of a diagnosed mental health disorder. A person can have a diagnosed mental health condition and still demonstrate meaningful levels of wellbeing if their condition is well-managed and they function effectively.
items.why: This distinction prevents a binary or stigmatising view of mental health and reflects the continuum model used throughout this topic.
items.example: Someone diagnosed with depression who attends therapy, maintains friendships, and holds down a part-time job may be placed toward the higher end of the mental wellbeing continuum, despite having a diagnosis.

items.title: I can define levels of functioning in the context of mental wellbeing
items.what: Levels of functioning refers to the degree to which an individual can complete day-to-day tasks in an independent and effective manner. It is an important indicator of overall mental wellbeing.
items.why: This is a directly assessable key term in the VCE study design. Being able to state and apply the definition accurately is required for short-answer and multiple-choice questions.
items.example: Preparing meals, maintaining personal hygiene, attending school or work, and managing household tasks are all examples of day-to-day functioning that can be used to assess this dimension of wellbeing.

subtopic.name: Levels of Functioning
subtopic.what: Levels of functioning refers to the degree to which an individual can complete day-to-day tasks in an independent and effective manner. This subtopic explores what high and low functioning looks like, and why it matters as an indicator of mental wellbeing.
subtopic.why: Functioning is often the most observable indicator of mental wellbeing. Changes in a person's ability to carry out daily tasks can be an early warning sign that their mental wellbeing is declining.

items.title: I can describe characteristics of high levels of functioning
items.what: Individuals with high levels of functioning are able to carry out basic everyday tasks, be productive, set and pursue goals, adapt to environmental changes, and operate with independence where physically and developmentally appropriate.
items.why: Being able to describe high functioning with specific characteristics allows students to identify it in scenario-based exam questions and justify their answers with evidence from the scenario.
items.example: Maria wakes each morning, prepares breakfast, attends her university classes, submits her assignments on time, and adjusts her study schedule when unexpected events arise. This pattern reflects high levels of functioning.

subtopic.name: Levels of Functioning
subtopic.what: Levels of functioning refers to the degree to which an individual can complete day-to-day tasks in an independent and effective manner. This subtopic explores what high and low functioning looks like, and why it matters as an indicator of mental wellbeing.
subtopic.why: Functioning is often the most observable indicator of mental wellbeing. Changes in a person's ability to carry out daily tasks can be an early warning sign that their mental wellbeing is declining.

items.title: I can describe characteristics of low levels of functioning
items.what: Individuals with low levels of functioning may struggle to carry out basic tasks such as maintaining hygiene, feel persistently lethargic or unproductive, lack direction or the ability to set goals, and be unable to cope with environmental changes.
items.why: Recognising low functioning in a scenario is a common exam task. Linking specific behaviours to this concept demonstrates understanding beyond rote recall.
items.example: Tom has not showered in four days, is missing shifts at his job, and cannot decide whether to reply to a text message from a friend. These specific difficulties reflect low levels of functioning.

subtopic.why: Functioning is often the most observable indicator of mental wellbeing. Changes in a person's ability to carry out daily tasks can be an early warning sign that their mental wellbeing is declining.

items.title: I can explain why disability does not automatically mean low levels of functioning
items.what: The concept of functioning is relative to an individual's physical and developmental capacity. A person with a disability who successfully meets the demands of their daily life with appropriate support is still considered to have high levels of functioning.
items.why: This is a nuance explicitly noted in the course content and reflects ethical, non-stigmatising thinking about disability. It may appear in exam scenarios designed to test critical understanding.
items.example: A person who uses a wheelchair and relies on a support worker to assist with physical tasks, but who manages their finances, maintains friendships, and pursues personal goals, demonstrates high levels of functioning for their context.

subtopic.name: Levels of Functioning
subtopic.what: Levels of functioning refers to the degree to which an individual can complete day-to-day tasks in an independent and effective manner. This subtopic explores what high and low functioning looks like, and why it matters as an indicator of mental wellbeing.
subtopic.why: Functioning is often the most observable indicator of mental wellbeing. Changes in a person's ability to carry out daily tasks can be an early warning sign that their mental wellbeing is declining.

items.title: I can explain how low levels of functioning affect overall mental wellbeing
items.what: When an individual is consistently unable to meet the demands of daily life, this can create a cycle of hopelessness and reduced self-belief, which further lowers mental wellbeing. Low functioning reduces a person's sense of capability and control.
items.why: Understanding the feedback loop between functioning and wellbeing is important for extended-response questions that ask students to explain relationships between concepts, not just define them.
items.example: Ingrid, a new mother, begins to believe she is incapable of caring for her daughter after several days of sleep deprivation. Her reduced ability to cook, sleep, and respond calmly to her sister's offer of help reflects how low functioning can diminish self-belief and wellbeing.

items.title: I can define resilience as used in VCE Psychology
items.what: Resilience refers to the ability to cope with and manage change and uncertainty. It enables a person to overcome stressors and recover from challenges. Importantly, resilience does not mean the absence of difficulty or distress.
items.why: The exact wording of the definition matters in VCE. The study design specifies 'change and uncertainty' rather than 'difficulty' or 'problems', so using imprecise language can cost marks in phrasing questions.
items.example: A student who loses their part-time job and, after an initial period of distress, adjusts their budget, applies for new positions, and maintains their social connections is demonstrating resilience.

subtopic.name: Resilience
subtopic.what: Resilience is defined as the ability to cope with and manage change and uncertainty. This subtopic examines what high and low resilience look like, how resilience relates to coping, and whether resilience is fixed or learnable.
subtopic.why: Resilience is a key dimension of mental wellbeing in the study design and appears regularly in exam scenarios. It is also practically important for students navigating stressful periods such as VCE.

items.title: I can describe characteristics of high levels of resilience
items.what: A person with high resilience seeks solutions to problems, uses appropriate coping strategies, remains flexible when circumstances change, and maintains optimism and hope in the face of adversity.
items.why: Identifying high resilience in scenarios requires knowing its specific markers. Vague answers such as 'they coped well' are insufficient without reference to these characteristics.
items.example: After failing a practice exam, Mei Zhen consults her teacher, revises her study timetable, and continues attending study group sessions. She maintains hope that she can improve before the final exam. These behaviours reflect high resilience.

subtopic.name: Resilience
subtopic.what: Resilience is defined as the ability to cope with and manage change and uncertainty. This subtopic examines what high and low resilience look like, how resilience relates to coping, and whether resilience is fixed or learnable.
subtopic.why: Resilience is a key dimension of mental wellbeing in the study design and appears regularly in exam scenarios. It is also practically important for students navigating stressful periods such as VCE.

items.title: I can describe characteristics of low levels of resilience
items.what: A person with low resilience may experience enduring feelings of being overwhelmed, rely on unhealthy or unhelpful coping strategies, be unable to adapt to change, and lack hope or optimism.
items.why: Low resilience markers are tested in exam scenarios where students must identify and explain why a character is not coping effectively.
items.example: After a conflict with a colleague, Matisse spends two weeks ruminating, avoids returning to work, and turns to alcohol to manage her distress. These patterns reflect low resilience.

subtopic.why: Resilience is a key dimension of mental wellbeing in the study design and appears regularly in exam scenarios. It is also practically important for students navigating stressful periods such as VCE.

items.title: I can explain why high resilience does not mean a life free from stress or unhappiness
items.what: Resilience is about how effectively a person responds to and recovers from stressors, not about avoiding them. Resilient people still experience negative emotions and difficult events.
items.why: A common misconception is that resilient people do not feel distressed. Correcting this misconception is important for accurately interpreting scenarios and avoiding the error of dismissing distress as evidence of low resilience.
items.example: Despina is devastated by the death of her mother but still manages to organise the funeral, maintain relationships with her children, and complete household tasks. Her grief does not reduce her resilience.

subtopic.name: Resilience
subtopic.what: Resilience is defined as the ability to cope with and manage change and uncertainty. This subtopic examines what high and low resilience look like, how resilience relates to coping, and whether resilience is fixed or learnable.
subtopic.why: Resilience is a key dimension of mental wellbeing in the study design and appears regularly in exam scenarios. It is also practically important for students navigating stressful periods such as VCE.

items.title: I can explain how resilience relates to coping flexibility and self-esteem
items.what: High resilience is associated with high self-esteem, greater confidence in completing tasks, and increased coping flexibility. Coping flexibility refers to the ability to adjust coping strategies to suit different types of stressors, which in turn supports resilience.
items.why: The relationship between resilience, coping flexibility, and self-esteem is explicitly noted in the curriculum and can be tested in questions that ask students to explain the links between different concepts.
items.example: A student who, when stressed about an assignment, sometimes seeks peer support, sometimes takes a break to exercise, and sometimes breaks the task into smaller steps, is demonstrating coping flexibility that builds and reflects high resilience.

subtopic.what: Resilience is defined as the ability to cope with and manage change and uncertainty. This subtopic examines what high and low resilience look like, how resilience relates to coping, and whether resilience is fixed or learnable.
subtopic.why: Resilience is a key dimension of mental wellbeing in the study design and appears regularly in exam scenarios. It is also practically important for students navigating stressful periods such as VCE.

items.title: I can explain that resilience can be learned and developed over time
items.what: Resilience is not a fixed trait. Research by Joyce et al. (2018) supports the view that resilience can be taught and developed, often through seeking appropriate social support during stressful periods.
items.why: This point has practical and theoretical importance. It underpins many wellbeing interventions and challenges deterministic thinking about whether people can improve their mental wellbeing.
items.example: A school wellbeing program that teaches students problem-solving skills, encourages them to seek support from trusted adults, and provides strategies for managing uncertainty is directly building resilience in participants.

items.title: I can define social wellbeing
items.what: Social wellbeing is the ability for an individual to form and maintain meaningful bonds with others, and to adapt to different social situations. It includes having a strong support network and being able to communicate effectively.
items.why: This is an assessable definition. Exam questions may ask students to identify or explain social wellbeing using evidence from a scenario, so precise knowledge of the definition is necessary.
items.example: Tina, after joining an English class and a netball team, develops friendships, communicates more effectively with colleagues, and builds a local support network. These outcomes reflect improved social wellbeing.

subtopic.name: Social and Emotional Wellbeing
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers social wellbeing, defined as the ability to form and maintain meaningful bonds and adapt to social situations, and emotional wellbeing, defined as the ability to control and express emotions adaptively and understand others' emotions. It examines how these two dimensions are distinct but deeply interconnected.
subtopic.why: Social and emotional wellbeing are central to everyday functioning and are frequently tested in VCE exam scenarios. Understanding both separately and together prepares students for analysis tasks.

items.title: I can describe characteristics of high and low social wellbeing
items.what: High social wellbeing involves having a strong support network, forming and maintaining meaningful relationships, and communicating effectively. Low social wellbeing involves isolation, difficulty forming relationships, and poor communication with others.
items.why: Describing the two ends of social wellbeing with specific markers allows students to match scenario evidence to the correct level of social wellbeing in analysis questions.
items.example: Tom, after losing his job, maintained contact with former colleagues and relied on two close friends for help moving house. Despite his circumstances, this reflects high social wellbeing.

subtopic.name: Social and Emotional Wellbeing
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers social wellbeing, defined as the ability to form and maintain meaningful bonds and adapt to social situations, and emotional wellbeing, defined as the ability to control and express emotions adaptively and understand others' emotions. It examines how these two dimensions are distinct but deeply interconnected.
subtopic.why: Social and emotional wellbeing are central to everyday functioning and are frequently tested in VCE exam scenarios. Understanding both separately and together prepares students for analysis tasks.

items.title: I can define emotional wellbeing
items.what: Emotional wellbeing is the ability to appropriately control and express one's own emotions in an adaptive way, and to understand and respond to the emotions of others. It includes experiencing a wide range of emotions while expressing them at suitable times.
items.why: Emotional wellbeing is a distinct but related construct to social wellbeing. Confusing the two is a common error. Knowing the definition precisely allows for accurate and differentiated exam answers.
items.example: A person who feels angry during a workplace conflict but waits until a private meeting to raise the issue calmly, rather than reacting immediately, is demonstrating high emotional wellbeing through adaptive emotion regulation.

subtopic.name: Social and Emotional Wellbeing

It examines how these two dimensions are distinct but deeply interconnected.
subtopic.why: Social and emotional wellbeing are central to everyday functioning and are frequently tested in VCE exam scenarios. Understanding both separately and together prepares students for analysis tasks.

items.title: I can describe characteristics of high and low emotional wellbeing
items.what: High emotional wellbeing involves awareness of one's own and others' emotional states, experiencing a wide range of emotions, and expressing them appropriately. Low emotional wellbeing involves difficulty naming emotions, emotional numbness, or expressing emotions at inappropriate times.
items.why: These characteristics appear in exam scenarios. Students must identify whether a character is showing high or low emotional wellbeing and justify their answer with specific evidence.
items.example: Jimmy, after amygdala damage, showed less respect for colleagues and withdrew from family. His inability to regulate and express emotions appropriately reflects low emotional wellbeing.

subtopic.why: Social and emotional wellbeing are central to everyday functioning and are frequently tested in VCE exam scenarios. Understanding both separately and together prepares students for analysis tasks.

items.title: I can explain why social and emotional wellbeing are interrelated
items.what: Social and emotional wellbeing reinforce each other. The ability to understand and label one's own emotions enables communication of needs to others, strengthening relationships and social wellbeing. Conversely, empathy and understanding others' emotions supports the formation of meaningful relationships.
items.why: Questions often ask students to discuss social and emotional wellbeing together or to explain the connection between them. Understanding the mutual relationship between them enables more sophisticated responses.
items.example: A student who recognises that a friend seems upset (emotional awareness) and reaches out to check in (social behaviour) is demonstrating how emotional wellbeing supports social wellbeing in practice.

items.title: I can define the SEWB framework and explain what makes it multidimensional and holistic
items.what: The SEWB framework is a framework for wellbeing for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples that includes all elements of being. Multidimensional means it is made up of different components. Holistic means it considers the whole person, including mental, physical, spiritual, and social needs.
items.why: These two terms are specifically defined in the study design and are commonly tested. Students who conflate them or use them interchangeably will lose marks.
items.example: The SEWB framework is holistic because it does not treat mental health as separate from physical health, spiritual connection, or community. It is multidimensional because it identifies seven distinct sources of wellbeing, each of which contributes to the whole.

subtopic.name: SEWB Framework
subtopic.what: The Social and Emotional Wellbeing (SEWB) framework is a multidimensional, holistic framework for wellbeing developed specifically for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. It encompasses seven interconnected dimensions and acknowledges the role of social, historical, and political determinants.
subtopic.why: The SEWB framework represents a distinct and culturally grounded approach to understanding wellbeing that extends well beyond Western psychological models. It is directly specified in the VCE study design and must be understood both in its structure and its cultural significance.

items.title: I can identify and describe each of the seven dimensions of the SEWB framework
items.what: The seven dimensions are: Connection to Body, Connection to Mind and Emotions, Connection to Family and Kinship, Connection to Community, Connection to Culture, Connection to Country, and Connection to Spirituality and Ancestors. Each is interconnected and contributes to overall wellbeing.
items.why: Exam questions can ask students to identify specific dimensions or apply them to scenarios. Knowing all seven dimensions and their meanings is essential.
items.example: An Elder passing traditional language and ceremonial knowledge to younger community members addresses the Culture dimension. A community health worker visiting an isolated family member addresses the Community dimension.

subtopic.name: SEWB Framework

It encompasses seven interconnected dimensions and acknowledges the role of social, historical, and political determinants.
subtopic.why: The SEWB framework represents a distinct and culturally grounded approach to understanding wellbeing that extends well beyond Western psychological models. It is directly specified in the VCE study design and must be understood both in its structure and its cultural significance.

items.title: I can explain what Connection to Country means in the context of the SEWB framework
items.what: Country refers to the traditional lands of a particular language or cultural group, encompassing not only geographical boundaries but also the spiritual, emotional, and intellectual connections to and within those lands. In this framework, people belong to the land rather than owning it.
items.why: This concept is frequently misunderstood as simply referring to a geographic location. Understanding its cultural and spiritual depth is important for respectful and accurate exam responses.
items.example: An Aboriginal person who is displaced from their ancestral land and unable to participate in land-based cultural practices may experience reduced wellbeing in the Connection to Country dimension, affecting their overall SEWB.

items.title: I can explain what Connection to Spirituality and Ancestors means in the SEWB framework
items.what: Spirituality in this framework is a concept that connects all things and shapes beliefs, values, and behaviour. Ancestors are understood as interconnected with Creation spirits and Country, watching over, guiding, and protecting families and communities. This creates a sense of purpose and wellbeing.
items.why: This dimension is distinct from how spirituality is typically framed in Western psychology. Accurately representing it demonstrates cultural respect and conceptual precision.
items.example: The belief that ancestors provide guidance during difficult moments gives community members a sense of being protected and purposeful, contributing directly to their emotional and spiritual wellbeing.

items.title: I can explain the role of social, historical, and political determinants in the SEWB framework
items.what: The SEWB framework acknowledges that all seven dimensions of wellbeing for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples are impacted by social determinants (circumstances of living and working), historical determinants (legacy of colonisation and past policies), and political determinants (distribution of power and resources).
items.why: These determinants contextualise individual wellbeing within broader systemic forces. Ignoring them produces an incomplete understanding of SEWB and reflects a lack of critical awareness expected at VCE level.
items.example: The historical removal of Aboriginal children from their families (Stolen Generations) is a historical determinant that continues to affect Connection to Family and Kinship, Community, Culture, and Country for many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people today.

items.title: I can explain why the SEWB framework reflects a collectivist perspective
items.what: The SEWB framework is grounded in a collectivist worldview, meaning the self is understood as significantly linked to family and community rather than as a primarily independent individual. Cultural identity and connection to community are integral to wellbeing in this framework.
items.why: Understanding the collectivist foundation distinguishes the SEWB framework from many Western wellbeing models and explains why dimensions such as Family and Kinship and Community are central rather than peripheral.
items.example: In the SEWB framework, caring for an ill relative is understood as the responsibility of the wider family and community group, not just a biological parent or child. This reflects how wellbeing is communal and relational, not only personal.

It encompasses seven interconnected dimensions and acknowledges the role of social, historical, and political determinants.
subtopic.why: The SEWB framework represents a distinct and culturally grounded approach to understanding wellbeing that extends well beyond Western psychological models. It is directly specified in the VCE study design and must be understood both in its structure and its cultural significance.

items.title: I can explain why the SEWB framework acknowledges diversity within Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities
items.what: There is immense cultural and linguistic diversity among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Different groups and individuals may understand social and emotional wellbeing differently. The SEWB framework provides a broad shared structure while acknowledging this diversity.
items.why: Assuming all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples share identical beliefs is inaccurate and culturally disrespectful. This nuance is important for exam responses that discuss the framework's scope and limitations.
items.example: A student living in a remote community in the Northern Territory and an urban Aboriginal person in Melbourne may both draw on the SEWB framework but experience its dimensions very differently depending on their language group, proximity to Country, and access to community structures.

items.title: I can define the mental wellbeing continuum and describe its key features
items.what: The mental wellbeing continuum is a tool used to track fluctuating mental wellbeing, ranging from high levels to low levels. It is dynamic, meaning an individual's placement is not fixed and can shift over time in response to life circumstances.
items.why: This is a directly examinable definition. The word 'dynamic' and the idea that placement is not fixed are critical details that distinguish this model from categorical or diagnostic approaches.
items.example: A student who is thriving in Term 1 may shift toward the lower end of the continuum during exam period and return to the higher end after exams conclude. The same person occupies different positions on the continuum at different times.

subtopic.name: Mental Wellbeing Continuum
subtopic.what: The mental wellbeing continuum is a tool used to track fluctuating mental wellbeing, ranging from high to low levels. This subtopic covers what the continuum is, how it is used, and how internal and external factors influence where an individual is placed on it at any given time.
subtopic.why: The continuum model is fundamental to VCE Psychology's approach to mental wellbeing. It replaces a binary view of mental health and is required knowledge for interpreting scenarios and justifying placements on the continuum.

items.title: I can describe the characteristics of each point on the mental wellbeing continuum
items.what: At the high end, individuals function independently, cope with daily demands without excessive distress, and regulate emotions effectively. In the middle, individuals experience temporary disruption, difficulty concentrating, and amplified emotions. At the low end, individuals show high distress, are unable to meet daily demands, and may require professional diagnosis and treatment.
items.why: Exam scenarios typically ask students to place a character on the continuum and justify their answer. Knowing the specific characteristics of each zone allows precise, evidence-based justification.
items.example: Mei Zhen coping effectively with school SACs represents the high end. Mei Zhen unable to sleep during exam period but returning to normal afterwards represents the middle. Mei Zhen developing a diagnosed anxiety disorder with panic attacks and social withdrawal represents the low end.

subtopic.why: The continuum model is fundamental to VCE Psychology's approach to mental wellbeing. It replaces a binary view of mental health and is required knowledge for interpreting scenarios and justifying placements on the continuum.

items.title: I can define internal factors and give examples of how they influence mental wellbeing
items.what: Internal factors are factors that arise from within the individual. They include thought patterns, genetic predisposition, and the nature of an individual's stress response. These can either protect mental wellbeing or contribute to its decline.
items.why: Internal and external factors are specifically named in the study design. Students must be able to identify, define, and distinguish them, and apply them to scenarios.
items.example: A naturally optimistic thinking style (internal factor) can protect mental wellbeing by helping a person reframe a failed assessment as a learning opportunity rather than a catastrophe.

subtopic.why: The continuum model is fundamental to VCE Psychology's approach to mental wellbeing. It replaces a binary view of mental health and is required knowledge for interpreting scenarios and justifying placements on the continuum.

items.title: I can define external factors and give examples of how they influence mental wellbeing
items.what: External factors are factors that arise from an individual's environment. They include loss of a significant relationship, level of education, experiences at work or school, and access to support services such as medical and psychological treatment.
items.why: External factors are equally weighted alongside internal factors in the study design. Exam responses that focus only on internal factors will be incomplete.
items.example: Mei Zhen's access to a school counsellor (external factor) helped her maintain wellbeing during exam stress. Later, access to a psychologist (external factor) supported her recovery from an anxiety disorder.

subtopic.what: The mental wellbeing continuum is a tool used to track fluctuating mental wellbeing, ranging from high to low levels. This subtopic covers what the continuum is, how it is used, and how internal and external factors influence where an individual is placed on it at any given time.
subtopic.why: The continuum model is fundamental to VCE Psychology's approach to mental wellbeing. It replaces a binary view of mental health and is required knowledge for interpreting scenarios and justifying placements on the continuum.

items.title: I can explain how internal and external factors interact to influence mental wellbeing
items.what: Internal and external factors do not operate independently. They interact with each other, and the combination of multiple factors can either protect mental wellbeing or lead to its decline. A protective external factor can buffer the impact of a risk-increasing internal factor.
items.why: Questions that ask students to 'explain the influence of internal and external factors' require more than listing them separately. Showing how they interact demonstrates higher-order understanding.
items.example: Mei Zhen's genetic predisposition to anxiety (internal risk factor) contributed to her developing an anxiety disorder after university. However, her strong support network and access to a psychologist (external protective factors) supported her recovery.

subtopic.name: Mental Wellbeing Continuum
subtopic.what: The mental wellbeing continuum is a tool used to track fluctuating mental wellbeing, ranging from high to low levels. This subtopic covers what the continuum is, how it is used, and how internal and external factors influence where an individual is placed on it at any given time.
subtopic.why: The continuum model is fundamental to VCE Psychology's approach to mental wellbeing. It replaces a binary view of mental health and is required knowledge for interpreting scenarios and justifying placements on the continuum.

items.title: I can define stress and describe where it sits on the mental wellbeing continuum
items.what: Stress is a psychological and physiological experience that occurs when an individual encounters something of significance that demands their attention or efforts to cope. Stress is usually in response to a known cause. It fluctuates between medium and high levels of mental wellbeing depending on severity and duration.
items.why: Stress is the baseline concept from which anxiety and phobia are distinguished. Knowing its definition and placement on the continuum precisely prevents confusion with the other two constructs.
items.example: A student who feels stressed the night before a chemistry SAC but prepares, sits the test, and moves on is experiencing stress. It is a normal, known-cause response that does not persist and does not significantly disrupt functioning.

subtopic.name: Stress, Anxiety, and Specific Phobia
subtopic.what: This subtopic distinguishes between stress, anxiety, and specific phobia as examples of different placements on the mental wellbeing continuum. It examines the key psychological and biological differences between these three constructs, including their stimuli, emotional valence, adaptive value, and associated nervous system activity.
subtopic.why: Differentiating stress, anxiety, and phobia is a specific study design requirement and a common source of errors in exam responses. Precise, comparative knowledge of all three is essential.

items.title: I can define anxiety and describe where it sits on the mental wellbeing continuum
items.what: Anxiety is a psychological and physiological response involving feelings of worry and apprehension about a perceived threat. It is typically future-oriented and may be in response to an unknown stimulus. Like stress, it fluctuates between medium and high levels on the continuum but can move toward low levels if it becomes excessive and persistent.
items.why: Anxiety is frequently confused with stress in exam responses. The key distinguishing features (unknown stimulus, future-orientation, distress only) are testable and must be stated precisely.
items.example: Renata feels uneasy and worried about her school year but cannot identify a specific cause when asked by her parents. Her future-focused, cause-unknown distress is consistent with anxiety rather than stress.

subtopic.name: Stress, Anxiety, and Specific Phobia
subtopic.what: This subtopic distinguishes between stress, anxiety, and specific phobia as examples of different placements on the mental wellbeing continuum. It examines the key psychological and biological differences between these three constructs, including their stimuli, emotional valence, adaptive value, and associated nervous system activity.
subtopic.why: Differentiating stress, anxiety, and phobia is a specific study design requirement and a common source of errors in exam responses. Precise, comparative knowledge of all three is essential.

items.title: I can define specific phobia and describe where it sits on the mental wellbeing continuum
items.what: Specific phobia is a type of diagnosable anxiety disorder characterised by excessive and disproportionate fear when encountering or anticipating a particular stimulus. It is associated with low levels of mental wellbeing, is always maladaptive, and significantly disrupts daily functioning.
items.why: Specific phobia is the only one of the three constructs that is always placed at the low end of the continuum and is always maladaptive. This makes it distinctively testable.
items.example: Grace, who has feared heights since childhood, breaks down in tears and is unable to set foot on a bridge despite recognising that her fear is disproportionate. This persistent, diagnosable, functioning-disrupting response is consistent with specific phobia.

subtopic.name: Stress, Anxiety, and Specific Phobia
subtopic.what: This subtopic distinguishes between stress, anxiety, and specific phobia as examples of different placements on the mental wellbeing continuum. It examines the key psychological and biological differences between these three constructs, including their stimuli, emotional valence, adaptive value, and associated nervous system activity.
subtopic.why: Differentiating stress, anxiety, and phobia is a specific study design requirement and a common source of errors in exam responses. Precise, comparative knowledge of all three is essential.

items.title: I can compare stress and anxiety on the basis of stimulus type, emotional valence, and adaptiveness
items.what: Stress is typically in response to a known stimulus and can involve either positive (eustress) or negative (distress) feelings. It can be adaptive in the short term. Anxiety is typically future-oriented and may involve an unknown stimulus. It involves only distress and can be adaptive in small amounts but becomes maladaptive when persistent.
items.why: Comparison questions between stress and anxiety are a common exam format. Knowing at least two clear differences is necessary for a complete answer.
items.example: A student who is stressed about an upcoming presentation (known cause) but energised by it is experiencing eustress. A student who feels generalised dread about starting Year 12 without a clear source is experiencing anxiety.

subtopic.what: This subtopic distinguishes between stress, anxiety, and specific phobia as examples of different placements on the mental wellbeing continuum. items.title: I can explain why all three constructs involve sympathetic nervous system activation
items.what: Stress, anxiety, and specific phobia all involve the sympathetic nervous system becoming dominant, producing physiological responses such as increased heart rate, rapid breathing, increased perspiration, and dilated pupils. This is the biological component shared across all three.
items.why: The role of the sympathetic nervous system is a biological detail required for explaining the physiological dimension of these experiences. It is also a bridge to the biopsychosocial content in Chapter 9.
items.example: When Grace approaches the bridge, her sympathetic nervous system activates, producing rapid heartbeat, sweating, and rapid breathing. These same physiological responses occur in someone experiencing exam stress or pre-performance anxiety, though the trigger and severity differ.

subtopic.what: This subtopic distinguishes between stress, anxiety, and specific phobia as examples of different placements on the mental wellbeing continuum. It examines the key psychological and biological differences between these three constructs, including their stimuli, emotional valence, adaptive value, and associated nervous system activity.
subtopic.why: Differentiating stress, anxiety, and phobia is a specific study design requirement and a common source of errors in exam responses. Precise, comparative knowledge of all three is essential.

items.title: I can explain what makes specific phobia always maladaptive while stress and anxiety can be adaptive
items.what: Stress and anxiety in moderate amounts can motivate useful behaviour, such as preparing for an exam or being cautious in a new environment. Specific phobia is always maladaptive because the fear is excessive, disproportionate, and leads to avoidance that disrupts daily functioning regardless of context.
items.why: The adaptive versus maladaptive distinction is explicitly noted in the study design comparison table and is a high-value conceptual distinction for exam responses.
items.example: Mild anxiety before a job interview can motivate preparation and sharpen focus, making it adaptive. By contrast, a person with a specific phobia of elevators who refuses to attend job interviews on upper floors experiences a fear response that consistently disrupts their functioning, making it always maladaptive.

items.title: I can apply knowledge of stress, anxiety, and phobia to a scenario to justify a placement on the mental wellbeing continuum
items.what: To apply these constructs to a scenario, students must identify the nature of the stimulus (known or unknown), the emotional valence (eustress or distress), whether the response is disproportionate, whether it disrupts daily functioning, and how persistent it is. These criteria together determine placement on the continuum.
items.why: Scenario-based application is the highest-frequency question type in VCE Psychology exams for this topic. Being able to systematically work through these criteria ensures confident and accurate responses.
items.example: Rohan avoids skiing equipment and withdraws from family and friends two weeks after his uncle's death, with significant disruption to daily functioning. This pattern, if persistent and excessive, moves beyond ordinary stress or grief toward placement at the lower end of the continuum, warranting further consideration of whether a diagnosable condition is present.
